column3: A direct parallel: bodily members testify against their owner concerning what they used to do.
Worshiped beings become enemies and deny the worship, adding a secondary reversal of evidence rather than bodily testimony.
Divine knowledge of hidden things and vision of deeds gives the focus's testimony its all-knowing judicial horizon.
The sealing of hearing and covering of sight contrasts with the focus where those same faculties testify.
The immediately preceding gathering of God's enemies toward the Fire supplies the setting for the testimony.
Universal resurrection and divine hearing and sight give a broad setting, but add little after the immediate context.
Sealed hearts, hearing, and sight explain a prior failure of the faculties later called as witnesses.
The direct continuation records the skins' answer and grounds their capacity to testify.
Hearing and sight are bestowed within human testing, giving their later testimony a responsibility context.
The threatened removal of hearing and sight is only a figurative contrast to the witnessing faculties.
Night, daylight, hearing, and seeing form a general sign discourse without a judgment or testimony link.
It joins skins to the Fire's bodily punishment, complementing the focus's skin as a witness.
Granted hearing, sight, and hearts prove ineffective amid denial, a useful antecedent to their later testimony.
The direct explanation says they did not conceal themselves from their own hearing, sight, and skins.
Skins respond to revelation in a living devotional sense, a distant contrast to their forensic speech here.
Repeated refusal distorts hearts and sight, supplying a moral path toward the judgment scene.
Denial of the Hereafter and withholding zakah belong to the surah's opposition but do not clarify testimony.
God as sufficient witness supports the judicial logic, though it is less specific than bodily witnesses already seen.
Recompense for deeds states the consequence principle but adds no evidence mechanism.
A clear messenger and failed remembrance form remote warning context only.
Deeds losing weight at resurrection connects action to final assessment, but not to embodied testimony.
The driving of disbelievers to Hell and their admission supply a closely related final-judgment scene.
The next immediate verse identifies their false assumption about God as the cause of their ruin.
Fearful eyes and sharp tongues in a worldly conflict do not illuminate eschatological testimony.
The contrasting procession into Paradise gives an outcome contrast, but no witness relation.
Steadfast believers and angelic reassurance offer a later-surah contrast to the condemned speakers.
God sees what people do and knows hidden movements, reinforcing the comprehensive knowledge behind the testimony.
Seeing a future outcome is too general to add to the focus's evidentiary event.
Solomon's ordered gathering shares only the word for mustering, not the Fire or testimony setting.
God's witness over everything supports accountability generally, now redundant beside more direct witness verses.
At death they testify against themselves as disbelievers, a useful human self-testimony parallel.
The earlier rejection of messengers supplies distant surah background rather than the testimony mechanism.
The nullification of deeds by association states a consequence but adds little to witnesses and evidence.
Sudden seizure after ignored reminders is a warning pattern, not a direct link to the focus's scene.
Friends becoming enemies on that day offers a general reversal in judgment without testimony.
Divine hearing and sight amid cosmic alternation are too general after stronger knowledge parallels.
The arrival of what was promised supplies only a bare eschatological horizon.
The clarified Arabic Book is remote from the bodily testimony in the focus.
It explicitly promises that disbelievers will be informed of what they did and taste severe punishment.
Repeated blindness and deafness despite repentance, under God's sight of deeds, develops culpable misuse of faculties.
The Hour and failure of alleged partners form nearby judgment context but do not add to the witnesses.
The person is described as a witness concerning his conduct, providing a concise self-testimony parallel.
God sees what people do after hostilities cease, a general accountability statement already well covered.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are divinely given from birth, supplementing their later accountability.
God's perfect seeing and hearing of the unseen is a broad redundancy rather than a new testimony relation.
God gives life and death and sees deeds, but the verse concerns worldly regret about battle deaths.
Doubt about meeting the Lord and divine encompassing knowledge provide only a broad nearby frame.
Upholding one's testimonies concerns faithful public witness, not organs testifying against a wrongdoer.
Authorized intercession through knowing truthful testimony is a legal contrast, but not close to the focus.
The mustering of deniers resembles the setting but is redundant after 41:19 and lacks testimony.
God's witness over all things repeats the general divine-witness theme without bodily specificity.
Divine sight during a historical siege does not clarify the focus's judgment evidence.
Rejecting the Reminder is distant surah background rather than a link to the testimony scene.
The disciplined vision in the heavenly encounter does not add to culpability or testimony.
Prompt repentance after wrongdoing contrasts with the focus's irreversible exposure at judgment.
The final question asks what they were doing after their denial, linking deeds to judgmental interrogation.
Hearing, sight, and hearts as entrusted gifts, and failure to give thanks, sharpens their moral accountability.
The legal requirement for four human witnesses in slander is not the eschatological bodily testimony at issue.
Persistent disbelief in a divine revelation is nearby opposition context only.
A messenger serves as a witness against a people, adding a distinct external witness alongside the body's witnesses.
Public witnessing of a worldly legal punishment and skin lashes only loosely parallels the focus.
God's hearing and knowledge in seeking refuge concern present temptation, not final evidence.
Hidden allegiance is disclosed through deeds under God's awareness, supporting the action-to-evidence logic.
Witnessing the month of Ramadan is a different legal sense of shahida.
The decree falls because of wrongdoing and leaves them unable to speak, contrasting with the speaking organs in the focus.
Lightning nearly taking sight is a natural sign with no judgmental testimony connection.
God, angels, and people of knowledge testify to divine unity, a different object of testimony.
Deafness and blindness toward revelation offer a nearby antecedent to the sensory accountability in the focus.
Witness and witnessed are too compressed and unspecified to add beyond earlier testimony passages.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify for what people earned, an exceptionally close organ-witness parallel.
A witness is raised from each community and disbelievers cannot make amends, extending the final-hearing setting.
Present sons as a blessing use a different sense of being witnessed or present.
A hidden reward proportionate to deeds offers a favorable recompense contrast, now marginal.
Companions beautify what is before and behind them, supplying a remote cause of loss in the same surah.
Forgiveness and gardens reward workers, a broad favorable contrast to accountable wrongdoing.
The release of Gog and Magog shares only an arrival-and-opening phrase without evidentiary relevance.
Their invoked partners vanish and they realize there is no escape, continuing the surah's judgment outcome.
The command to watch and a future seeing does not clarify witnessing against deeds.
Calling God alone under distress and abandoning partners supplies a distant contrast to final accountability.
The creation and adornment of the heavens do not bear on the focus's witnesses.
The challenge whether they fail to see is a rhetorical denial scene, not evidence from organs.
The appearance of immortal youths in Paradise is unrelated.
Nothing is hidden from God and people will be requited for what they do, a close nearby accountability frame.
God repays evildoers and good-doers according to their deeds, supporting the judgment for which testimony is given.
Noah refuses knowledge of followers' deeds, a limited contrast that leaves such judgment to God.
God knows what messengers do, but the instruction on wholesome food and righteous action is remote.
The abode of peace is tied to what they used to do, a broad favorable outcome contrast.
Tongues claim what hearts do not hold while God knows their deeds, a useful contrast between self-report and true evidence.
Questioning about what they did is relevant but too terse to add much after explicit judgment passages.
Successors are tested by how they act, an earthly accountability precursor only.
The deafening blast signals the Last Day but offers no witness or deed relation.
Unseen divine nearness at death does not clarify bodily testimony against actions.
Miserly wealth is physically encircled at resurrection, a specific consequence but not an evidentiary link.
Signs within selves and a call to see loosely resonate with the body as evidence, but remain general.
Threatened return to another religion is a worldly coercion scene.
Humbled eyes reveal fear at resurrection, a bodily response but not testimony of deeds.
In Hell they plead to be returned for different deeds and are refused, closely framing irreversible accountability for prior action.
Pharaoh's call to listen is a historical rhetorical question unrelated to final witnesses.
The brothers' concern about loss despite their group has no connection to the focus.
Repentance voiced only at death after persistent evil is rejected, strongly delimiting the focus's belated exposure and consequence.
Each person's deed-record is brought forth open on the Day of Resurrection, directly supplying a durable evidence counterpart to the body's testimony.
The person is commanded to read his own record and is sufficient as his own reckoner, closely matching self-implicating judgment.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each held responsible, directly clarifying why the focus's hearing and sight can testify.
The opened record misses no small or great deed, and people find what they did present before them.
Just scales are set for Resurrection and even the weight of a mustard seed is brought forward for reckoning.
A truthful record speaks against or for people without injustice, providing a written-evidence parallel.
God writes what people sent ahead and their traces, making past action an enduring record before resurrection.
The Book is set down and prophets and witnesses are brought when judgment is made in truth.
Every soul is repaid in full for what it did under God's complete knowledge of deeds.
On that day every soul is repaid for what it earned and no injustice occurs.
Messengers and believers are aided on the day when witnesses stand, expanding the eschatological witness setting.
God hears secret counsel and private conversation while messengers record it, pairing divine knowledge with a written record.
Every community is summoned to its record while kneeling, an explicit final-account scene.
The two receivers record everything uttered and done at a person's sides, adding a concrete evidentiary mechanism.
No word is spoken without a ready watcher recording it, a close parallel to inescapable testimony.
Each soul comes with a driver and a witness, directly extending the judgment process around the focus.
God raises them, informs them of what they did, and has counted actions they themselves forgot.
Receiving the record in the right hand depicts the personal disclosure of one's account at judgment.
Receiving the record in the left hand supplies the contrasting condemned-account outcome.
A person is informed of what he sent ahead and left behind, directly connecting remembered action to final disclosure.
The human being is a witness against himself even while offering excuses, a particularly close self-testimony parallel.
Human excuses cannot displace the self-evidence already established in the preceding verse.
Everything has been enumerated in a record, reinforcing comprehensive preservation of deeds.
The scrolls are spread open in the final scene, supplying the disclosure of recorded evidence.
Noble guardian-recorders are appointed over people, establishing external preservation of their acts.
The recording guardians are explicitly described as writers, strengthening the evidence-record theme.
The guardians know what people do, linking deed knowledge to the preceding recorders.
Receiving one's record in the right hand adds the favorable form of individual judgmental disclosure.
Receiving the record from behind one's back adds the condemned form of that disclosure.
The earth tells its reports on that day, a striking nonhuman-witness parallel to the speaking skin and senses.
The earth's reporting follows divine inspiration, closely paralleling the skins' claim that God made them speak.
Even an atom's weight of good is seen, clarifying the exhaustive scope of the deeds under testimony.
Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, likewise sharpening the focus's accountability for action.
What is in graves and breasts is brought out, adding inward disclosure to the focus's outward bodily evidence.
Humans and jinn confess against themselves that worldly life deceived them, a direct self-confession in a final summons.
God is a witness over every undertaking and no deed escapes the encompassing record, joining observation to inscription.
Witnesses declare God's curse on wrongdoers in the final setting, supplying another explicit judgment witness.
A witness is raised from every community and the Book is brought, broadening the final evidentiary assembly.
Every soul finds its good and evil deeds present before it, directly expressing the persistence of action for judgment.
A witness from every community and the messenger as witness establish a parallel formal testimony scene.
What is disclosed or concealed is brought into God's reckoning, supporting the focus's rejection of hidden wrongdoing.
The Fire remains their abode and no appeasement is accepted, immediately extending the consequence of the testimony scene.
